keywords: how to undo commit in git
title: How to Undo the Last Git Commit (Keeping Changes)
answer: To undo your last Git commit while keeping all your changes staged in the working directory, run: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. To unstage the changes as well, use `git reset HEAD~1`.
highlights: Keep Changes Staged: git reset --soft HEAD~1
Keep Changes Unstaged: git reset HEAD~1 (or git reset --mixed HEAD~1)
Discard Changes Permanently: git reset --hard HEAD~1
Undo Already-Pushed Commit: git revert HEAD (creates a new safe commit that inverts changes)

keywords: difference between git rebase and merge
title: Git Rebase vs Git Merge — Key Differences & Best Practices
answer: Git merge creates a new merge commit preserving exact history and branch topology. Git rebase rewrites project history by moving or applying your feature branch commits sequentially on top of the target base branch, creating a clean, linear commit log.
highlights: Git Merge: git merge feature_branch (Non-destructive, creates merge commit, preserves exact timeline)
Git Rebase: git rebase main (Linear history, rewrites commit SHA hashes)
Golden Rule: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a public/shared branch

title: Git Stash Commands — Saving & Restoring Uncommitted Work
answer: Git stash temporarily shelves (or stashes) changes you've made to your working copy so you can switch branches without committing unfinished work: `git stash` saves changes, and `git stash pop` restores and removes the most recent stash.
highlights: Save Changes: git stash (or git stash save "message")
Save Untracked Files: git stash -u (or --include-untracked)
Restore & Delete from Stash: git stash pop
Restore & Keep in Stash: git stash apply
List Stashes: git stash list | Delete All: git stash clear

title: Git Cherry-Pick — Applying Specific Commits Across Branches
answer: Git cherry-pick applies the changes introduced by one or more existing commits to your current HEAD branch: `git cherry-pick <commit-hash>`. It is useful for porting bug fixes across release branches.
highlights: Single Commit: git cherry-pick <commit-hash>
Multiple Commits: git cherry-pick <hash1> <hash2>
Range of Commits: git cherry-pick <start-hash>..<end-hash>
Abort on Conflict: git cherry-pick --abort | Continue: git cherry-pick --continue

title: HTTP Status Code Reference (1xx, 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx)
answer: HTTP status codes indicate the result of a client request. Categorized into: 1xx (Informational), 2xx (Success), 3xx (Redirection), 4xx (Client Errors), and 5xx (Server Errors).
highlights: 200 OK / 201 Created / 204 No Content: Successful request execution
301 Moved Permanently / 302 Found (Temporary Redirect) / 304 Not Modified: Cache validation
400 Bad Request / 401 Unauthorized (unauthenticated) / 403 Forbidden (no permission) / 404 Not Found / 429 Too Many Requests
500 Internal Server Error / 502 Bad Gateway / 503 Service Unavailable / 504 Gateway Timeout

title: Difference Between var, let, and const in JavaScript
answer: var is function-scoped and hoisted with undefined. let and const are block-scoped ({}) and reside in a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) before declaration. const cannot be reassigned after initialization.
highlights: var: Function-scoped, hoisted to top with undefined, can be redeclared and updated in same scope
let: Block-scoped, hoisted into TDZ (throws ReferenceError if accessed early), reassignable
const: Block-scoped, TDZ protected, cannot be reassigned (though object properties can still be mutated)
Modern Standard: Prefer const by default; use let when value must mutate; avoid var

title: JavaScript Closures — Definition, Scope & Practical Applications
answer: A closure is the combination of a function bundled together with references to its surrounding state (lexical environment). In JavaScript, closures give an inner function access to an outer function's scope even after the outer function has executed and returned.
highlights: Definition: Inner function retains access to outer variables via lexical scoping chain
Primary Uses: Data privacy/encapsulation (private variables), function factories, currying, event handlers and callbacks
Memory Note: Retains references to outer scope variables, preventing garbage collection until closure is released

title: JavaScript Event Loop — Call Stack, Microtasks & Macrotasks
answer: The JavaScript Event Loop is a single-threaded concurrency mechanism that continuously monitors the Call Stack and Task Queues. If the Call Stack is empty, it flushes all Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) before executing the next Macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O).
highlights: Call Stack: Executes synchronous JavaScript code frame by frame (LIFO)
Microtask Queue (High Priority): Promise.then/catch/finally, async/await continuations, MutationObserver
Macrotask Queue / Task Queue: setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate, I/O, UI rendering
Execution Order: Synchronous code → All microtasks in queue → Single macrotask → Repeat

title: JavaScript Promises & Async/Await Reference
answer: A Promise represents the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation and has 3 states: Pending, Fulfilled, or Rejected. Async/await provides synchronous-looking syntax over Promises.
highlights: Promise.all([p1, p2]): Resolves when all resolve; rejects immediately if any promise rejects (fail-fast)
Promise.allSettled([p1, p2]): Waits for all promises to settle and returns an array of results with status and value/reason
Promise.race([p1, p2]): Settles with the outcome (resolve or reject) of the first promise to settle
Promise.any([p1, p2]): Resolves with first fulfilled promise; rejects only if all reject (AggregateError)

keywords: how to write list comprehension python
title: Python List Comprehension — Syntax & Examples
answer: List comprehension in Python offers a concise way to create lists based on existing iterables: `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`. It is faster and more readable than standard for-loops with append.
highlights: Basic Syntax: [x**2 for x in range(10)]
With Filter Condition: [x for x in numbers if x % 2 == 0]
If-Else Conditional: [x if x > 0 else 0 for x in numbers]
Dict Comprehension: {k: v for k, v in zip(keys, values)} | Set: {x for x in data}

title: Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)
answer: The Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a mutex used by the CPython interpreter to synchronize thread execution so that only one native thread executes Python bytecode at a time, preventing memory race conditions in CPython's reference counting.
highlights: Mechanism: Mutex lock ensuring thread safety in CPython memory management
CPU-bound Tasks: Standard threading does not achieve multi-core parallelism (use `multiprocessing` or native C-extensions instead)
I/O-bound Tasks: Threading works well because GIL is released during I/O operations (network, disk, sleep)
Python 3.13+: Introduction of experimental free-threaded mode (PEP 703: disabling the GIL)

title: Python Decorators — Syntax & Implementation
answer: A decorator in Python is a higher-order function that takes another function as an argument, extends or alters its behavior without modifying its source code, and returns the modified function: `@decorator_name` above a `def` definition.
highlights: Syntax Sugar: `@my_decorator def func(): ...` is equivalent to `func = my_decorator(func)`
Pattern: Takes `func`, returns `wrapper(*args, **kwargs)`
Preserving Metadata: Use `@functools.wraps(func)` on wrapper to preserve original `__name__` and `__doc__`
Common Built-ins: `@staticmethod`, `@classmethod`, `@property`, `@lru_cache`

title: Docker Essential CLI Commands Cheat Sheet
answer: Docker provides containerization tools to build, ship, and run applications in isolated environments. Essential commands include: `docker run`, `docker build`, `docker ps`, `docker exec`, and `docker-compose`.
highlights: Run Container: docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name my_app image_name
Build Image: docker build -t image_name:tag .
List Running Containers: docker ps (or docker ps -a for all)
Interactive Shell in Container: docker exec -it <container_id> /bin/sh (or bash)
Stop & Remove: docker stop <id> && docker rm <id>
Prune Unused Data: docker system prune -af

title: SQL Joins Explained (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, CROSS)
answer: SQL joins combine columns from one or more tables based on related columns: INNER JOIN (matches in both tables), LEFT JOIN (all left rows + matched right rows), RIGHT JOIN (all right rows + matched left rows), FULL OUTER JOIN (all rows when match in either), and CROSS JOIN (Cartesian product).
highlights: INNER JOIN: Returns rows where join condition matches in both Table A and Table B
LEFT (OUTER) JOIN: Returns all rows from Table A and matching rows from Table B (NULL if no match)
RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN: Returns all rows from Table B and matching rows from Table A
FULL (OUTER) JOIN: Returns rows when there is a match in either Table A or Table B
CROSS JOIN: Produces Cartesian product (Row count = A × B)

title: ACID Properties in Database Management Systems (DBMS)
answer: ACID is a set of four key properties that guarantee database transactions are processed reliably: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (preserves database rules and constraints), Isolation (concurrent transactions execute independently), and Durability (committed changes survive system crashes).
highlights: A - Atomicity: Entire transaction succeeds or entirely rolls back (no partial commits)
C - Consistency: Transaction transforms database from one valid state to another satisfying all schema constraints
I - Isolation: Intermediate state of a transaction is invisible to other concurrent transactions (Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable)
D - Durability: Once a transaction is committed, data persists permanently even after power loss (WAL/logging)

title: SOLID Principles in Object-Oriented Software Design
answer: SOLID is an acronym for five design principles for maintainable, scalable software: S (Single Responsibility), O (Open/Closed), L (Liskov Substitution), I (Interface Segregation), and D (Dependency Inversion).
highlights: S - Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): A class should have only one reason to change
O - Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification
L - Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP): Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering program correctness
I - Interface Segregation Principle (ISP): Many client-specific interfaces are better than one general-purpose interface
D - Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): Depend upon abstractions (interfaces), not concretions
